newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Telecom deal puffs life into Kazakh privatisation.
newsitem.headline: Telecom deal puffs life into Kazakh privatisation.

text.p: A deal giving South Korea's Daewoo Corporation rights to a 40 percent stake in Kazakhstan's telecoms monopoly put wind in the sails of the ex-Soviet state's privatisation programme.

"We chose to give exclusive negotiating rights to Daewoo Corporation," Kazakh Finance Minister Alexander Pavlov told a news conference after Monday's agreement, saying the company had offered $1.37 billion for the share in NAK Kazakhtelekom's ageing telecoms network.

Daewoo beat South Korea's Hanwha, Germany's Siemens AG, Alcatel Alstrom SA unit Alcatel Sel AG, Malaysia's Usaha Tegas Sdn Bnd and British Virgin Islands registered Kaztel Investment Group for the tender.
Daewoo has promised the government, hunting for cash to pay of a mountain of unpaid wages and pensions, a $100 million bonus.
Daewoo has said it will also pay off a 390 million mark debt to German investment agency Kreditanstalt fur Wiederaufbau and the government's outstanding $40 million telephone bill to Kazakhtelekom.

Daewoo's executive director, Kim Bong-Bu, said the company would invest the remaining one billion dollars in Kazakhtelekom, saying the existing two million lines would be increased to 3.3 million by 2000.

"A telephone will be as widespread as running water or electricity," Kim said, perhaps unaware the government has problems in providing the latter to many of the 16.9 million population scattered across an area of steppe the size of western Europe.

Foreign investors question the Kazakh government's commitment to its high speed sale of state-owned enterprises and utilities after several tender results collapsed almost as quickly as they were announced in recent weeks.

Tuesday's deal is already THE second time around for Kazakhtelekom after a framework agreement signed last year with Germany's Deutsche Telekom AG for management control and a 49 percent stake in the monopoly fell apart in December.
Investors also complain of a lack of transparency in the tender process and widespread corruption.

"Kazakhstan will work with any company which offers the best conditions," said Pavlov, defending Kazakh privatisation. "I think there has been real transparency in the privatisation process in the last one and half years."

Most strategic investors also insist on management control, a threat to Soviet-era "red directors" who have fought against relinquishing control to foreign companies, especially in the republic's embattled but potentially wealthy oil sector.
Daewoo must hammer out an agreement with the government on management control before the contract's final signing at the end of May.
But Kazakhtelekom Chairman Serik Burkitbayev ruled out full control for Daewoo. "The question of management is still a question but they (Daewoo) will not have full control," he said.
